best.rationale: x2 connects persistent backdoors in ref-008 with the case for white-box auditing in ref-016, proposing an activation classifier and neuron-masking intervention on a defined experimental setting. Its evaluation needs controls distinguishing recognition of the year from detection of an unsafe mechanism, and it mischaracterizes adversarial training as a detection baseline. Nevertheless, its grounding is stronger than y2's: ref-005 already investigates adversarial safety and does not describe the existing adversarial-training methods y2 attributes to it. y2's actual contribution—training a defense using ensemble-generated perturbations—is useful and testable, but its stated gap substantially misrepresents its sole reference.

worst.rationale: y3 largely repeats ref-002, which already uses hypothetical corporate environments, replacement and goal conflicts, and test-versus-deployment self-assessment. Activation clustering offers a possible difference, but 'latent intent' lacks an operational definition. Still, its environments and behavioral measurements fit together. x3 provides no interface connecting physical patches against manipulation policies in ref-005 to corporate language-agent scenarios from ref-002. Toxicity scores from ref-006 also do not establish detection of blackmail or information leakage. These mismatches make x3 less executable and its results harder to interpret.

diversity.rationale: Y offers three substantively different directions: distillation-data mitigation, adversarial robustness training for robotic policies, and corporate-agent evaluation. X covers distinct failure modes, but x1 and x2 share neuron-based detection and intervention, while x3's inclusion of physical attacks lacks a coherent experimental role. Y's robotics defense therefore adds more genuine methodological and application diversity.

overall.rationale: Although x2 is the strongest individual option, Y provides a more useful selection overall. y2 has a concrete defense experiment beyond the attacks in ref-005, and y1 pairs distillation with identifiable political-bias and reasoning evaluations grounded in refs-009, ref-010, and ref-014, despite underspecified interventions. x1 additionally treats FACET as a distillation framework, assumes an unexplained teacher-to-student neuron correspondence, and attributes bias scores to ref-003's categorical framework. Combined with x3's incompatible components, this leaves X with fewer workable choices. Y's gap claims still require substantial correction, especially y3's overlap with ref-002.
